title: The Educated Barbarian: An introduction to Stoicism (Enchiridion analysis part 4)
summary: Fourth Enchiridion episode: insults only hurt if you accept them, anyone pursuing growth must expect ridicule from their own circle, living to please others costs you your purpose, and money should be earned without selling your principles. NH relates it to his family discouraging his attempts to get bigger and to relationships testing a man's individuality.
claims: Insults only hurt because of your own opinion about them; the goal of stoicism is to negate the attack entirely, not just pretend not to care
The situation is neutral: two people in the same situation react differently, so the emotion comes from you; easy to understand, hard to apply
Freeing yourself from outside preoccupations leaves far more mental energy for worthwhile things
Anyone trying to rise will be pulled down by peers (crabs in a bucket); this also impairs class mobility in poor neighborhoods
When he was trying to get bigger, family members told him it was a waste of time and he would never get big
Being mean is the weak-minded lowering others' potential so they never have to fulfil their own; bulletproof yourself by expecting it
Those who mocked you will admire you if you keep going and succeed, and your rise can elevate them too
A strong community is built from strong individuals through emulation; if you believe in the collective, be a strong individual
Paradox of the group: the group needs individuality but tries to crush it; an individual who fails returns weakened and gets ridiculed twice as much
The moment you live your life to please others you have lost your purpose, since others do not have your best interest at heart
In relationships, partners test whether you will change on demand; holding firm to who you are usually makes them happier in the long run
Women in particular test a partner extensively to ensure he will not leave at the first difficulty, especially with children in view
Making money is fine and capitalism is good, but selling your principles for useless wealth means money owns you
Money is the true number one religion in the world
Money is a symbolic trade of energy and time; it is a necessary evil, and anti-capitalists err in calling it evil in itself
If you abandon your values to make excess money, the person you were making money for no longer exists
